parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-īˀnas, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos. Cognate with Lithuanian -inas and Proto-Slavic *-inъ.

parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-kos, *-ḱos. Cognates include Lithuanian -ingas, Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ, *-kъ, Proto-Germanic *-gaz, Latin -icus, Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós), Sanskrit -शस (-śasa), -कस (-kasa).

parole.significato: Usually found on verbs (and their derived nouns or adjectives) with the meaning 'around' or 'about' (like German um- or…
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi, *h₁opi.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- Cognate with Lithuanian ar (“whether, if, and”), Ancient Greek ἄρα (ára, “then”).

parole.significato: cold (an object or substance that has a relatively low temperature)
parole.testo: Alteration of austs ‘cooled’, past participle of dialectal aũsīt, aũsēt ‘to cool off, down’, ausināt (“to cool off hot food, with a spoon”) (compare Lithuanian áušti (“to cool down”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ewǵ- (compare Latin autumnus, Old Irish úacht, Old Armenian ոյծ (oyc)). The -k- may be
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰh₂- (“to burrow, dig”), see also bads (“hunger, starvation”).
Per Karulis, an intra-Baltic formation, an iterative of bilst, which, in turn, from bilt. Per Derksen, formed as such already in PIE, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥d-.

parole.significato: to utter; to say, especially in few words
parole.testo: Underlyingly *bild-ti, an iR-vocalization of the zero-grade *bʰl̥- of Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound; to speak, roar, bark”) which gave rise to an (unattested) *bilt which was extended with an additional -d- giving bilst. Of the same origin as balss (“voice”). Cognate with Lithuanian bilti (“

parole.significato: to go, to ride (in a vehicle)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewk- (“to stroke, to rub”) (whence also brukt, q.v.), from a stem *bʰer- (“to cut, to rub, to split; to hit”) (whence also berzt, q.v.). The meaning evolution was probably: “to scrub, to grate” > “to rub, to wipe” (a meaning still conserved in the erstwhile iterative for

Cognate to Lithuanian bùrė (“sail”). Ultimately perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bʰew- (“to swell”) (whence also bozt) with a suffix -rā- whence Proto-Baltic *burā- whence the Latvian term with the initial meaning of “that which inflates”. It is possible that the Lithuanian term is a borrowi

parole.significato: pale (with lighter, whiter color on the face or skin than normal; without redness; also, implicitly, unhealthy)
parole.testo: Originally a parallel form to an older adjective *bals (which disappeared probably because of homophony with balss “voice,” but left related terms like the verbs balot, balēt “to bleach, to fade,” balināt “to whiten, to blanch”), from the same source as the adjective balts (“white”) (q.v.). Note tha
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-o-s, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.
From Proto-Indo-European *kelH-m- (“stump”), a depalatalization of *ḱélh₂-m(on)-; cognate with Lithuanian kélmas (“stub, shrub, beehive”), Proto-Germanic *helmô (“handle; helm, tiller”).

parole.significato: village, settlement (small group of houses that forms a territorial unit)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱeym- (“village, home”) (whence also saime (“family, household”), q.v.), from *ḱey-, *ḱoy- (“to be located; camp; abode”); the original meaning of ciems was thus “camp, encampment.” A parallel form *kaims (> kaimiņš (“neighbor”), q.v.) also existed. Since Proto-Indo-Europea

parole.significato: dense, tight (with component parts that are linked or very close to each other)
parole.testo: From the same stem as Latvian ciets (“hard, solid”), from which it was a variant yo-stem: Proto-Indo-European *key- (“to set in motion, to move”) with a variant -tyo-s of an (adjectivizing) suffix -to-s > Proto-Baltic *keityas > *kietyas > ciešs. It is also possible that the adverbial form cieti of

According to Derksen, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰr̥Hbʰ-, a zero-grade of *(s)dʰerHbʰ- (“to exert force”). Cognate with dir̂bt (“to walk fast”), Lithuanian di̇̀rbti (“to work”), Proto-Germanic *derbaną (“to work”). An older theory by Karulis derives the term from Proto-Baltic *darbas, fro

parole.significato: to do (to carry out, to realize something, to be busy with something)
parole.testo: Originally the iterative counterpart of an earlier verb *dert (“to tear, to split”), from Proto-Baltic *der-, from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to split, to tear, to peel”). The meaning evolved as follows: “to tear, to split” > “to cut, to chop (wood)” (cf. the derived form darināt kokus “to pear, to

From Proto-Indo-European *der-, *dr- (“to tear, rip, split”) (whence also dīrāt (“to skin, flay”)), with a suffix *-eh₂, yielding *dr-eh₂ > drā-, and another suffix, either *-no-/*-nā-, or (according to Pokorny) *-p-an, with the p later reducing to zero (but still conserved in the Lithuanian and San

parole.significato: twin (a boy born together with another child from one mother)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, twofold”) (with an extra suffix *-no, *-nyo), from *dwi- (“two”), whence also divi (“two”) (q.v.). Cognates include Lithuanian dvynỹs, Old High German zwiniling (< *twi-na-), German Zwilling, English twin, Latin bini (“in twos, in pairs”) (< *dwis-no-).

From Proto-Indo-European *gʰelgʰ- (“iron”) (which was apparently borrowed from Asia Minor). Initially the Latvian reflex was dzelzis, which still exists (as a masculine, 2nd declension, usually plural noun) with the meaning “piece(s) of iron”. Cognates include Lithuanian geleži̇̀s, Old Prussian gels

parole.significato: expensive, costly (having a high price, for which one must pay very much)
parole.testo: There are differing suggestions on the origin of this term, the most likely of which is to derive it from Proto-Indo-European *der-, *dor- (“to tear, to peel, to pluck, to slice”) (whence also dergties (“to feel disgusted”), q.v.), with an extra gʰ, from which Proto-Baltic *darg- > *dargs > dārgs (w
Derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”), whence also Latvian dȩ̄̂ls (“son”). Cognate with Lithuanian dėlė̃.
Usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂lek- (“to protect”), but it could instead be from a non-Indo-European substrate language. Comparable to Lithuanian alkas, Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌷𐍃 (alhs, “temple”).

parole.significato: I; first person pronoun, referring to the speaker
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēź-, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵ (from *éǵh₂). The non-nominative forms derive from Proto-Indo-European dependent stem *me- (the a instead of e in the Baltic languages appears to result from Iranian influence): reduplicated *me-me- → *mene → Proto-Baltic genitive/accusative

parole.significato: rooster, cock (male domestic fowl, especially Gallus gallus)
parole.testo: From *gal-n-o, enlargement of *gl̥H-o, zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *golH-so. Cognates include Welsh galw (“call”), English call, Lithuanian gal̃sas (“echo”), Russian го́лос (gólos, “voice”), Polish głos (“voice”), Albanian gjuhë (“voice”)).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂- (“to go, step”), related to the past tense of iet.

From an old verb *gart (“to heat, to grow hot”), from the same stem as garša (“taste”) and gars (“spirit; vapor, steam”) (q.v.), all from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer-, with an extra suffix -d. The original meaning was presumably “heated” (e.g., cooked on a fire) > “prepared, ready” > “tasty.”
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“to burn, be warm”), see also Proto-Balto-Slavic *garḗˀtei.
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“hot, warm”), see also Welsh gwres (“heat”).

parole.significato: long (having a relatively great distance from one end to the other)
parole.testo: From a derived adjective *gar-is of a masculine form *garyas, parallel to old neuter form *garyan (“forest, tree”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *garā́ˀ, from the o-grade form *gʷorH-eh₂ of Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (> *h₁egʷr-), meaning “mountain, peak” and secondarily “forest” (via, e.g., “mountain s

parole.significato: ready (such that it has reached its final or desired state, form; such that it has been prepared, completed)
parole.testo: This word is traditionally considered (together with its Lithuanian and Old Prussian cognates) a borrowing from Slavic, itself, in turn, also traditionally seen as a borrowing from Germanic (Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍄𐌰𐌿𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gataujan) may have had a derived adjective *gataws). A more recent hypothesis is that the Sl
According to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *g⁽ʷ⁾ʰew- (“to perceive”), see also Proto-Germanic *gaumaz (“attention”), Proto-Slavic *gověti (“to fast”).

parole.significato: smooth (without much friction, without surface irregularities like bumps, holes, etc.)
parole.testo: From the same stem as the verb glaust (“to smooth, to pet”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *glewd-, *glūd, *glud (“to press, to smear, to stick”). An original Proto-Baltic u-stem *gludus was replaced in Latvian by a parallel o-stem form, from which came gluds, and a parallel yo-stem form, which gave ri

From the same stem as the verb gult (“to lie down”), of which it was originally the iterative (and possibly causative) form, from Proto-Indo-European *gwel- (“dwelling-place, hole”), see also Lithuanian guolis (“resting place”). Originally it was an i-stem, as can be seen in dialectal forms like gul
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“mountain”), see also Lithuanian gùras (“promontory”), Proto-Balto-Slavic *garā́ˀ (“forest”), Ancient Greek δεῖρος (deîros)).

parole.significato: or, also known as, to wit
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *Hyós, *Hye- (relative pronoun), with a particle ba, attested also at the end of the old conjunction neba. Cognates include Lithuanian jei (“if”), dialectal jeba.

parole.significato: strip, stripe (a narrow, elongated part of an object or a surface that differs from its surroundings)
parole.testo: From the same stem found in josta (“belt”), Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- (“to girdle”), but with a different suffix (-l(a) instead of -t(a)). Cognates include Lithuanian júoslas (“tie, bind, bandage”), and, with yet another suffix, Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “belt, sash, zone”) (from *zṓsnā from *yōs-

parole.significato: belt (a band worn around the waist, to keep clothes in place, to hold weapons, or serve as decoration)
parole.testo: From the same stem found in josla (“zone, strip”), Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- (“to girdle”), but with a different suffix (-t(a) instead of -l(a)). Cognates include Lithuanian júosta, Proto-Slavic *pojasъ (compare Russian пояс (pojas)), Sanskrit रास्ना (rā́snā, “girdle”) (< *yā́s-nā), Ancient Greek

According to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *ked- (“to fume, smoke”), comparable to Proto-Slavic *kaditi (“to burn incense”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *kádruš (“tan, brown”), Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar”). However, these words are all of uncertain origin.
From Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to hit, strike”), cognates include Latin clādēs. See the latter for more.

From the (intransitive) verb karst (“to heat up, to grow hot”) (q.v.), of which it is the past participle, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“to burn”), from which also Lithuanian kárštas (“hot”), Latin carbo (“coal”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌹 (hauri, “coal”).

parole.significato: to howl, to wail, to yowl
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *kū- (“to cry out, call, howl”). Cognate with Lithuanian kaũkti.

Cognates include Lithuanian kliẽpas (“loaf”), and possibly Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (English loaf, Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃 (hlaifs, “bread”), Proto-Slavic *xlěbъ). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn, move”) nominalized to mean "disk, wheel, circle" (from the same root also Latvian ka
From Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-. Cognate with Lithuanian klausýti.
From Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (“to hear”), similar to klàusît.

parole.significato: blackfly (small insects of the order Diptera (family: Simuliidae) that suck blood and resemble flies)
parole.testo: Derived from the verb knist (“to itch”) (q.v.). Some dialectal variants (knausis, knauslis, knusis) have the same basic root (Proto-Indo-European *ken-, *kn-), but with a different suffix and/or ablaut form.
From Proto-Indo-European *krewH- (“to heap up”). Cognate with Lithuanian krūvà (“pile, heap”).

parole.significato: left-hander, left-handed man (someone who is better with his left hand than with his right hand)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *sker-, *ker-, *kr̥- (“to turn, to bend”), changed to Proto-Baltic *krei-, with a suffix -r, giving rise to an adjective *kreiras > *kreilas (compare archaic adjective krails (“bent, crooked”)) and a noun *kreiris. The meaning evolved from “bent, crooked” to “not strong, clu

parole.significato: left, left-side (located on the side of the human body that contains the heart)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”), changed to *krei- (whence also kreilis (“left-hander”)), with a suffix -so. The meaning evolved from “bent, crooked” to “not strong, clumsy, weaker, less good,” hence “left (hand),” as opposed to the “good,” “able” right hand. Cognates include

parole.significato: rapids (section of a river where the water flows rapidly down, usually over or around rocks)
parole.testo: Related to the Latvian verb krākt (“to roar”). The most likely theory is that the word krāce was influenced by krākt (in, e.g., lengthening the ā), but that it originally was *krace, a form of dialectal kracis (“pole with crossbar (for drying grain)”), from Proto-Indo-European *krek-, *krok- (“to st

From Proto-Indo-European *krū̆t- (“protuberance, breast, belly”), probably related to *krew- (“curve”), *(s)ker- (“to turn”), *(s)krew-. Possibly related to Old Irish crott (“lute”), Proto-Germanic *hraukaz (“pile, stack”), but these connections are uncertain.

Morphologically from kuce (“female dog”) + -ēns. Karulis, however, considers this to be the primary term and kuce its derivative. From Proto-Indo-European *kew- : *kū̆- (“to swell; to bend (over)”), whence also Latvian kukt (“to hunch one's back”). Development of meaning "round" > "such that rolls a

From Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to hit, strike”) thence also Latvian kal̃t. From a parallel form of the root Proto-Indo-European *kol- in its reduced grade Proto-Indo-European *kl̥- > Proto-Baltic *kul- whence this term. Cognate with Lithuanian kùlti.
From Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to turn, move”). However, according to a different view (Endzelīns, Fraenkel, Blese, Urbutis, Karaliūnas) etymology 2 is the same as etymology 1.

From a parallel form *kurt of the (old) verb kurst (“to be(come) pierced, hollow, torn”), derived with an extra -l (cf. also the dialectal form kursls, from kurst), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”). The semantic evolution was: “with holes, hollow” > “having ears with holes, mutilated

Per Karulis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷr̥mis [thus a doublet of Proto-Balto-Slavic *kirmis (“worm”), whence Lithuanian kirmis, Latvian ķirmis, cirmenis (“woodworm, grub”)] Karulis also mentions ķirmis and the e-grade cērme (“roundworm, parasitic nematode”) as cognates, he also points to Finnish ku
From Proto-Indo-European *kweth₂- (“to foam, bubble”)

parole.significato: stomach (extension of the digestive tract between the oesophagus and the small intestine)
parole.testo: From earlier guņģis (“belly”) by dissimilation, from Proto-Indo-European *geng- (“lump”), from the stem *gen- (“to squeeze, to make (something) round”). See also Latvian dziedzeris (“gland”).

parole.significato: craving, covetous, thirsty or hungry (in the figurative sense)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *keh₂- (> Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂-ro-s > Proto-Baltic *kāras). Cognates include Old Norse hórr, Gothic 𐌷𐍉𐍂𐍃 (hōrs, “adulterer”) (from *hōra-), Sanskrit चारु (cā́ru, “pleasant, lovely”), Latin cārus (“dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: hook (object with a curved, sharp tip used for suspending or hanging)
parole.testo: The origin of this word is not clear. It may stem from Proto-Indo-European *ḱāk-, *ḱak- (“branch, pole”), via metathesis (from *kāḱ- to Proto-Baltic *kāš- to Latvian kāsis), with the original meaning being “bent branch.” Cognates would then include Lithuanian dialectal kóšis, and maybe also Sanskrit

parole.significato: happiness (mental and emotional state denoting harmony with the internal and external worlds; the quality of one who is…
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Indo-European stem as the verb laist (“to let, to allow”) (q.v.): *laid-mē > laime. The verb laist can also mean “to give, to grant,” which would suggest for laime the original meaning of “given, granted (thing),” which could be either positive or negative, i.e., “fate,” a meanin

parole.significato: nice, polite, kind, friendly, warm, welcoming (one that treats others with attention, sensitivity, kindness, friendline…
parole.testo: From the same stem as the verb lipt (“to stick, to adhere”) (q.v.), from which it was derived (with vowel gradation, like laipa (“footbridge”), and an extra n; compare, without vowel gradation, the dialectal variant lipns). The semantic evolution was probably “sticky, adhesive” > “clingy” > “attenti
From Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ-. Compare to Lithuanian laižyti and Russian лизать (lizatʹ).

Traditionally related to Latvian lāse (“drop (of liquid)”) (dialectally attested as lase, lasis), perhaps because of the drop-like little spots on a salmon's scales, from Proto-Indo-European *laḱ- (“to sprinkle, to spatter”). Another suggestion is that this term comes from Proto-Indo-European *lek-
From Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.

parole.significato: big, large (being more than the size of other similar objects, creatures, etc.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *lei- (“to decrease, to disappear; thin, slim, slender”) (maybe from the stem *el- (“hungry”)), with an extra suffix -l. The semantic development was probably: “thin, slender” > “long, tall (big in height)” > “remarkable because of size, significance”. A more recent suggesti

parole.significato: shin (part of the leg from the knee to the ankle; syn. apakšstilbs, stilbs)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *lei- (“to bend”), from the stem *el- (“to bend”), whence also elkonis (“elbow”); compare also laiva (“boat”), leja (“valley”). The original meaning was probably “bending, curvature.” A similar semantic development can be seen in Sanskrit आणिः (āṇiḥ, “leg above knee”) (< *ar
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“illness”).
From Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.

Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂p- (“to shine”) and so cognate with Old Norse leiptr (“lightning”), Lithuanian liepsnà (“flame”), Ancient Greek λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”), Lithuanian lópė (“light”), Latin limpidus (“bright”).

parole.significato: slow (which moves so as to cover relatively small distances in every time interval)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *lēnas, Proto-Indo-European *leh₁-en-os, from *leh₁- (“to let, to allow”) (whence also Latvian laist (“to let, to allow”), q.v.). The semantic evolution was probably: “which is allowed (to do something)” > “not dangerous, gentle, calm” > “slow.” Cognates include Lithuanian lė
Cognate with Lithuanian lýgus (“flat, even; equal”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“alike, similar”). Further related to English like and -ly.
From Proto-Indo-European *ley-, *lī- (“to pour, to flow, to drip”).

parole.significato: vagina, vulva (a woman's external sexual organs)
parole.testo: From the same stem as maks (“purse, pouch”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *mak- (“(skin) bag, sack”), with an extra suffix -t. Cognates include Lithuanian makšti̇̀s.
From Proto-Indo-European *ml̥Hdʰo-, see also Breton malvenn, Old English molda (“forehead”), Ancient Greek βλωθρός (blōthrós, “lofty”), Avestan 𐬐𐬀-𐬨𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬜𐬋 (ka-mər^əδō, “demon's head”).

parole.significato: to search for, to look for (something or someone lost, hidden, etc.)
parole.testo: The origin of this word is not clear. Some researchers link it to Latvian mācēt (“to know how, to be able to”), Russian dialectal намо́кнуть (namóknutʹ, “to become accustomed”), Polish dialectal makać (“to touch, to hit”), maklać, makłać (“to touch”). Others suggest that meklēt comes from Proto-Indo

Nominal derived from an old (unattested) verb *melt, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, to crush, to pound”). The semantic evolution was probably: “something ground, crushed (to small pieces)” > “(unimportant) blabber, gossip” (a meaning attested for the verb malt in some contexts; compare

parole.significato: swampy, boggy, marshy, miry (typical of swamps, bogs, marsh, mires)
parole.testo: From the same stem as the verb mukt “to sink (in mud)” (q.v.), with an extra element -l, from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slimy, slippery”), see also Ancient Greek μύκης (múkēs, “mushroom”). Additional cognates include Lithuanian muklùs, Serbo-Croatian mùkljiv.

From Proto-Indo-European *mnt-, *ment- (“to chew; jaw, mouth”). Cognate with Latin mentum (“chin”) and mandō (“to chew”), Ancient Greek μάσταξ (mástax, “jaws, mouth”) and μασάομαι (masáomai, “to chew”), Welsh mant (“jawbone”), Hittite [script needed] (mēni, “chin”), Proto-Germanic *munþaz (“mouth”)

parole.significato: sister (a daughter of a couple, in relation to their other children)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *mā-, a baby language word for “mother,” “mommy” (whence also mãte, q.v.). This word, probably at first a term of endearment, has replaced an earlier descendant of Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (still found in Lithuanian sesuõ, genitive form seser̃s). Cognates include Lithuani

parole.significato: month (one of the 12 divisions of the year)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), from *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognates include Lithuanian mė́nuo (“month, moon”), Old Church Slavonic мѣсѧць (měsęcĭ, “moon, month”) (whence Russian ме́сяц (mésjac), Polish miesiąc, Czech měsíc), Sanskrit मास (māsa), Persian ماه (mâh), Old Armenian ամ

parole.significato: moon (largest satellite of the Earth; often Mēness)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognates include Lithuanian mė́nuo (“month, moon”), Old Church Slavonic мѣсѧць (měsęcĭ, “moon, month”) (Russian ме́сяц (mésjac), Polish miesiąc, Czech měsíc), Sanskrit मास (māsa), Persian ماه (mâh), Ol
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₃neyd- (“to insult”).

parole.significato: is not; third-person singular present indicative of nebūt
parole.testo: Reduced form of navaid from nevaid (both still attested in Latvian dialects), originally the negative form of vaid (“to be located, to be”). (G. F. Stenders, in his 1774 grammar, mentions under nevaid the reduced forms neva, nava and even nav' with an apostrophe.) This form replaced an earlier neir,

parole.significato: wild, furious, raging (having a propensity to attack)
parole.testo: From an unattested verb *nikt, similar in meaning to the Lithuanian cognate (see below; compare also Latvian dialectal verb nikties (“to annoy, to disturb”)), formed with an extra -n (compare verb īgt, adjective īgns); *nikt is derived from Proto-Indo-European *nēyk-, *nik- (“to attack, to start qui

parole.significato: nostril (one of two openings at the bottom of the nose)
parole.testo: From Proto-Balto-Slavic *nāsis, from Proto-Indo-European *nās-, an allomorph of *nas- (“nostril”). Semantic changes from “nose” to “nostril” or vice-versa were frequent in Indo-European. Cognates include Lithuanian nósis, Old Prussian nozy ([nōsi]), Sudovian nasis ([nāsis]) “nose”, Proto-Slavic *nos
From Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃syos, from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃s-. Cognate with Lithuanian uosis.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁óh₃s. Compare Lithuanian úostas.
From Proto-Indo-European *neyH- (“to make butter, churn”), and cognate with Persian پنیر (panīr).

parole.significato: gray (having the color of, e.g., ash; white with low brightness)
parole.testo: Traditionally derived from pele (“mouse”) (q.v.), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“gray, pale”), with a suffix -ek, to refer to an inherent quality of mice. But maybe it was derived directly from *pel-, via a previous adjective *pels (whence the verb pelēt (“to grow moldy, mildewy”) and the dialecta

parole.significato: sleeve (part of a garment that covers one's arms)
parole.testo: Originally a variant of a regularly derived piedurtne, from the verb piedurt (“to pin, to attach (with a pin)”), ultimately derived from pie-, from Proto-Indo-European *préy (“at, near”)) + durt (“to stab, prick”) + -ne. The original meaning was thus “something attached, sewn (on something else).”
From Proto-Indo-European *pel-, *pʰel, *spʰel- (“to cleave, to split off, to cast off”). Cognate with Lithuanian plėšti.
From Proto-Indo-European *pret- (“to understand”). Cognate with Lithuanian prõtas. See prast for more.

parole.significato: swamp, bog, marsh, morass (low wetland with a layer of accumulated peat)
parole.testo: The origin of this word is unclear, but probably Proto-Indo-European. Some compare it to Lower Sorbian para (“filth, dung”), Polabian poro (“filth, dung; swamp, bog”) (assuming that o < *uo < *ō), from a stem *pōr- to which an extra v or vo was added. Others relate purvs to Ancient Greek πυρρός (pur
From Proto-Indo-European *pew- (“to blow (up)”), see also Ancient Greek φῦσα (phûsa), Latin pustula.
From Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

An old compound, with as first part Proto-Indo-European *per- (“over”), and the second part a different term in different Indo-European languages (in Ancient Greek and Sanskrit, the second term was probably *ut- < *wet- (“year”), i.e., *per-ut(i)-). Of onomatopoeic (imitative) origin, as is the case with several other Indo-European bird names, all from Proto-Indo-European onomatopoeic *pī- (reduplicated form *pīp-): Samogitian pīlė (“duck”), Bulgarian пи́ле (píle, “chick, young bird”), Serbo-Croatian pȉle (“chick”), Slovene pípa (“chicken”), An

parole.significato: to chat, to chatter, to babble, to gossip (to talk about minor, unimportant topics)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *bel-, *pel-, *bla-, *pla-, an onomatopoeic stem that imitates human speech. Apparently, this stem was reduplicated in pļāpāt and underwent expressive palatalization (pl > pļ). Cognates include Lithuanian plõpti, pliõpti, pliopóti, German plappern.

From Proto-Indo-European *pew- (“to blow (up)”), see also Lithuanian pupa (“bean”), Lithuanian pū̃sti (“to blow”), pūslė̃ (“blister, bladder”), Norwegian føysa (“to swell”), Proto-Slavic *puxàti (“to blow”), Latin pustula (“bubble”).

Although Karulis does not list this word, it is very likely cognate with pūst (“to blow, inflate”) or pūt (“to rot”) from Proto-Indo-European *pū- (“to rot, swell, become bloated”). -pūte would be the standard way of nominalizing the verb pūst (from its past stem pūtu) for neologism coining purposes

parole.significato: to find (to cause by searching that something (desirable, necessary) be present, in use, or in one's possession)
parole.testo: This word is the reflex of two different Proto-Indo-European forms: *wer-d-, *wr-ed- (“to bend, to sway”) and *werdʰ-, *wr-edʰ-, *h₃erdʰ- (“to grow; high”), both from the stem *wer- (“to bend, to turn”). Both forms yielded Proto-Baltic *red-, *rad-, from which *rad-ti > *rasti > rast. The present te

parole.significato: wheel (circular device that rotates on its axis)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *ret(h), *rot(h). Cognates include Lithuanian rãtas (“wheel”), Sanskrit रथ (ratha, “chariot”), Old High German rad (“wheel”) (German Rad (“wheel”)), Latin rota (“wheel”) (Portuguese roda, Spanish rueda, Italian ruota, Romanian roată, French roue), Albanian rreth (“hoop, circ

parole.significato: rough, harsh, uneven, rugged (having an irregular, not smooth, harsh surface)
parole.testo: From an earlier adjective *raupus (yielding two parallel forms, a yo-stem form that became standard raupjš and an o-stem form that yielded the archaic noun raups), from the o-grade form *roup- of Proto-Indo-European *reup-, *rūp-, *rup- (“to pull, to tear, to break”) (from the *rup- form comes the a
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to roar, belch”), see also Icelandic jórtra (“to ruminate”), Old English rocettan (“to burp”).

parole.significato: speech, speaking, talking (articulated production of language)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *reu-, *ru-, imitative of speech sounds (from which also Latvian rūkt (“to roar, growl, snarl”), Russian рычать (ryčatʹ, “to roar, growl, snarl”)) with a suffix *-nā. Cognates include Old Irish run, Gothic 𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌰 (rūna, “secret, mystery”) (i.e., that which is said as a secret)

The origin of this word is unclear. It is possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *rew-, *rū-, *ru- (“to run, to rush”), via a previous adjective *runs, *rūns, on the model of brūns (“brown”), bruncis (“brown, bay horse”) (a variant of brūnis). Others have suggested that runcis is related to runa

parole.significato: coarse, rough (with elements having a relatively large cross section)
parole.testo: From an earlier adjective *rupus (yielding two parallel forms, a yo-stem form that became standard rupjš and an o-stem form that yielded the dialectal variant rups), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to pull, to tear, to break”) (whence also the adjective raupjš, q.v.). The semantic evolution was p

parole.significato: instrument, tool, equipment (an object used for a specific task, work, etc.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *rey-, *rī- (“to scrape; to pluck; to cut”) (with an extra k); cf. dialectal riekt (“to cut (bread); to plow (for the first time)”). Apparently, the original meaning of rīks was “sharp instrument,” perhaps “knife.” Cognates include Lithuanian rỹkas (“instrument; container”).

parole.significato: bittered; indefinite past passive participle of rūgt
parole.testo: From the same stem as the verb rūgt (“to ferment, to turn sour, bitter”), of which it is technically the past participle, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to retch, vomit, puke”), see also Old English rocettan (“to burp”). Cognates include Lithuanian rūgštùs (“sour”); cf. also 17th-cen

From Proto-Indo-European *ḱak- (“branch, stick”) (whence also sakne (q.v.)) from Proto-Indo-European *kek- / *ḱek- / *kekʰ- / *ḱekʰ-. Cognate with Lithuanian šaka (“branch”). Semantic development: branch > parting place of two branches > the two beams around a horse's neck. Along with šak- > sak-, t
From Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“cold; hot”). Cognates include Lithuanian šálti.

parole.significato: saliva (secretions of the glands in the mouth)
parole.testo: From the same stem as slieka (“earthworm”) (q.v.), with dissimilation (*sliekalas > siekalas); note dialectal forms like sliekas (“saliva”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sley- (“slimy, slippery, glide”). The synonymous word slienas comes also from the same stem, but with an extra n instead o

From Proto-Indo-European *sh₂ey- (or *sēy-), past sēju from an unchanged *sēy-, some dialects also have present seju from a short *sey-, otherwise present sienu from a no-stem with *ey > ie shift. Iterative saistīt (“to link”) via ablaut.

parole.significato: warm (with moderately high, generally pleasant temperature)
parole.testo: From the (intransitive) verb silt (“to warm up, to grow warm”) (q.v.), of which it is the past participle, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-; cognate with Latin caleō (“to be warm”).

parole.significato: to hit, to strike, to beat (move a body part or an object in order to touch so as to inflict pain, injury or death; to…
parole.testo: The origin of this word is not entirely clear. It has been compared with Ancient Greek κεντέω (kentéō, “to prick, to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱent- (“to pierce”): its zero grade *ḱn̥t would have yielded Proto-Baltic *šint-, whence Latvian sīt-, probably the stem of archaic term sīts (“hun
Apparently derived with -ēns from a no longer extant noun stem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *suH-. Compare Russian свинья́ (svinʹjá), English swine.

parole.significato: to be, become sad, to sadden, to feel sadness, sorrow, to grieve
parole.testo: The origin of this word is unclear. One possibility is that it a form of the dialectal verb kumt “to bend, to stoop,” from Proto-Indo-European *kew-, *ku- “to swell, to bend” with an extra -m. The initial s would result from variation, as in the case of kumšķis ~ skumšķis (q.v.). The original meanin

From the same stem as slieka (“earthworm”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *ley- (“humid, mucous, sticky, slippery, smooth”). The semantic evolution was probably “sticky, slippery” > “smooth” > “thin” > “tall, slender”.

parole.significato: to become wet, to get wet
parole.testo: According to Pokrony, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlep- (“wet, swampy”), see also Czech and Slovak slota (“rainy weather”), Lithuanian šlapias (“wet”), Ancient Greek κλέπας (klépas).
From Proto-Indo-European *sleh₂gʷ- (“to mishandle, press”), see also Ancient Greek λώβη (lṓbē, “disgrace”).

parole.significato: to smile (to produce a smile, a facial expression with the ends of one's mouth raised and the teeth shown, in order to…
parole.testo: From the verb smiet (“to laugh”) (q.v.), of which it was originally the iterative form (cf. skriet (“to run”), skraidīt (“to run around, several times”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mey-.
From Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μύλη (múlē), Old Norse mǫlr, Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“soft, mild”).
From Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μύλη (múlē), Old Norse mǫlr, Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“soft, mild”).
Originally the past passive participle of spirgt (“to become fresh, lively”) (q.v.). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sperg-.
From Proto-Indo-European *steyp- (“to be stiff, erect”), see also Latin stīpō (“to compress”), Lithuanian sti̇̀pti (“to stiffen”).

parole.significato: firm, strong, rigid (capable of resisting the actions of mechanical forces without harm or change)
parole.testo: From the same stem as the verb stingt (“to harden, to stiffen”) (q.v.), with an extra (adjectivizing?) r. A parallel form without the r yielded stings (“stiff, numb”). Cognates include Lithuanian stiñgras (“firm, strict”), stingrùs, sti̇̀ngrus (“rigid, stiff, numb; hard, solid; strained; heavy”). Th

From a 17th-century verb straut (“to flow, to float”) (later replaced by straust (“to flow quickly, to stream”)), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”), with an epenthetic t (whence also straujš (“quick, fast”)). Cognates include Lithuanian sraũtas (“stream, current, flow”) (dialectal straũtas

parole.significato: arrow, dart (projectile thrown with a bow)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *strel-, *strēl-, from *ster- (“line, streak, stripe; jet, spurt; beam”) (whence also Latvian stars (“ray, beam”), q.v.) with an extra l. The same stem also yielded the 17th-/18th-century verb strēlēt (“to shoot”), later replaced by šaut (“to shoot”). The basic meaning must

parole.significato: silver (precious metal; chemical element, with atomic number 47.)
parole.testo: From a late Proto-Indo-European root common to Balto-Slavic and Germanic for “silver”, not attested in other branches of Indo-European, likely borrowed from a non-Indo-European substrate. Cognates include Lithuanian sidãbras, dialectal sudãbras, archaic sidrabas (compare Latvian dialectal forms suda

parole.significato: brush (instrument made with flexible bristles attached to a handle, used especially for grooming hair)
parole.testo: There are competing theories on the origin of this word. The first (and more probable) one assumes that it comes from Proto-Indo-European *suH- (“pig”) > derived form *suk- “pig” (masc., fem.), “coarse hair, bristle” (neut.). Originally suka was the neuter plural form, but it became feminine singula

parole.significato: juice (liquids found in fruits which people can drink)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *sewh₁-leh₂, from *sewh₁- (“to press”). Direct cognates include Lithuanian sulà (“juice, sap”), Old Prussian sulo (“curdled milk”), Proto-Indo-Iranian *súraH (“intoxicating liquor”).

There are three main hypotheses on the origin of this word: (a) from the same source as sveķi (“resin”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *sʷekʷ-os (“juice, resin”), whence Proto-Baltic *sʷek-as > *sveke, plural *sveki with a number of variants, among which svece; (b) from an earlier *zvece, cognate with

There are divergent hypotheses on the origin of this word. Some suggest a connection with Old Norse sveigr (“flexible, nimble”), from Proto-Indo-European *swey- (“to bend, to turn, to swing”); with an extra -ko-s, one obtains Proto-Baltic *swey-ka-s, whence sveiks, originally “flexible, agile, nimbl
From Proto-Indo-European *sweyd- (“to sweat”)
From Proto-Indo-European *sweid-, from *swey(g)- (“to bend, swing”), see also Old English swican (“to move about”), Proto-Germanic *swiką (“deception, trickery”).
From Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-, similar to sviêdri.

From Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to put in line, in sequence, to tie, to assemble”), referring to the assembling of the wood for a bonfire, whence also sērt (“to stack, pile grain (to dry)”) and sers (“grain to be threshed (in the barn)”) (q.v.); sārts is derived from the verb with vowel gradation (

parole.significato: to suck; to absorb, to pump (to cause liquids, gases, etc. to move by rarefying the air inside some instrument, body pa…
parole.testo: This word results from the conflation of two independent stems: Proto-Indo-European *sew-, *sū-, *su- (“juice, moisture; to press juice; to suck”) with an extra -k, yielding Proto-Baltic *sūk- > Latvian sūk-; and Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to drain, to dry up, to fall (water)”) with an infix n, yie
From Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- (“to flow”); compare tecēt (“to flow, trickle”). Cognate with Lithuanian tãkas.
Cognate with Lithuanian tikti. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to be suitable”), cognate with Gothic 𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌽 (þeihan), Proto-Germanic *þinhaną.
From the same stem as the verb trunēt (“to decay, to rot”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *trew-, *tru- with a suffix lo (> la in Proto-Baltic).

parole.significato: to hold (to keep something that was taken, grabbed, in a fixed position, e.g., in one's hands, lap, back, etc.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *tur-yé-ti, from Proto-Indo-European *twerH- (“to enclose, grab”). In other words, from the same stem as tvert (“to grasp, to grab”), of which it was originally the iterative-durative form. (It is also possible that there was a semantically close verb *turt, from the same st

In principle, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *apē-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep-, *h₂op- (“(flowing) water, river”). Cognates include Lithuanian ùpė, dialectal ũpė, upi̇̀s, ùpis, Old Prussian ape (“river”), apus (“(water) well”), Sudovian upa (“river”), Hittite ẖap(a) (“river”), Sanskrit आपः (āpaḥ, “wat

parole.significato: louse, lice (many species of small insect parasites, all in the order Psocodea)
parole.testo: Usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *wēt-, *wet-, *ut-, from the stem *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”) (whence also Latin vējš (“wind”), q.v.) with a suffix -t. J. Endzelīns, connecting this word to Old Prussian wutris (“blacksmith”), and noting the ancient link between the notions of “forging” and “pricki

parole.significato: used to express emotional responses: excitement, surprise, pain, fear, sorrow, irritation, etc.
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“oh!, ah!; woe!, alas!”). Cognates include Lithuanian vái, vai̇̃, Old High German wē, Old English wā, Latin vae, German weh, English woe.
From Proto-Indo-European *welk- (“to pull, draw, drag”), here probably influenced by Proto-Indo-European *welg- (“humid, wet”); see Latvian valgs (“moist, humid, damp”).

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to tear, to spend”). Cognates include Latgalian volūda (“id.”), Lithuanian valandà (“hour, moment, time”). Alternatively related to Proto-West Slavic *volati (“to call”). Confer Polish wołać, Czech volat.
From Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-i-e-, extended from *welH- (“to roll”).

parole.significato: light, lightweight (which is not heavy, has low weight, low mass)
parole.testo: This word apparently resulted from the merging of two independent etymologies: (a) the same stem as liegs (“gentle, tender”), whose older form *liegvs apparently underwent metathesis to yield viegls, and (b) Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, to bend”) with an extra g, yielding *weyg-, from which
From Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- (“to pursue, hunt”), see also Proto-Slavic *vitati, Proto-Germanic *waiþō.

Underlyingly *virt-ti, an iR-vocalization of the zero grade version of Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn; to become”). The original meaning of the verb was "to become" (without any negative connotations.)

Underlyingly *vird-ti. Same origin as Latvian virt (“to bubble, boil”) (verdu, virdu) Lithuanian virti (“to boil”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to boil”), with the infinitive from zero grade and present from full grade. As the modern izvirst has been relegated to outbursts or eruptio

parole.significato: Germans (people from Germany; members of the German people; the German people as a whole)
parole.testo: Cognates include Lithuanian vókietis. There are different theories about the origin of this word. Some suggest that it comes from a place name, Latvian Vāca, Lithuanian Vókia, which would originally have referred to some region in Sweden, from which the word was borrowed, probably before the 12th ce

From Proto-Indo-European *wāy-, *way- (“weak”), perhaps derived from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Initially there were u- and o-stem forms (compare Lithuanian dialectal vójus (“weak, sick”), Latvian dialectal vājs); ultimately replaced by a yu-stem variant, yielding standard language vājš. The origin of this word is unclear. One suggestion links it, because of the burbot's moist, slimy skin, to Old Norse vǫkr, Ancient Greek ὑγρός (hugrós), Latin ūvidus (“moist, wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“wet, to water”), with the gʷ changing to g (so as to yield Latvian dz). Another sugg

parole.significato: ox (male cattle, usually castrated, often used as a beast of burden)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *wers-, *wr̥s- (“male”). Cognates include Lithuanian ver̃šis (“calf; (dialectal) ox”), Old Prussian werstian (“calf”) (maybe *wersistian?), Sanskrit वृष (vṛṣa, “bull; male”), वृषन् (vṛṣan, “man; stallion, ox”), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬭𐬱𐬥𐬌 (varšni, “ram”), Latin verrēs (“boar”).

From Proto-Indo-European *ǵen-, *ǵnō-, *ǵneh₃- (“to know, to recognize”) (whence also zināt, q.v.), possibly of the same origin as *ǵenh₁- (“to create, to generate”) (> “to give birth”, “to have/be a relative”). The initial meaning of znots was apparently “(new) relative”, “man who married into the
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu-, *ǵénus. Compare the root *ǵonh₂dʰos. Compare also Lithuanian žándas (“chin”), Old Prussian żauna (“jaw”).

parole.significato: sparrow (a number of bird species of the order Passeriformes, genus Passer)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *werb-, *werp- ( + -ulis; compare also vērpt (“to spin”)), from *wer- (“to turn, to twist, to bend”) (with an extra suffix -p, -b). The original meaning was a bird that turns and moves all the time. The initial z is either from an s-mobile, or the influence of some other ter
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-. Cognate with Lithuanian gilė.

parole.significato: exterior, outside (the space in the outside of a building, house, etc.)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *ar-, *arə- (“to plow”) (compare Latvian art), whence also the lexicalized variant āre (“open space; cultivated land”) and the verb art (“to plough”). The adverb ārā (“outside”) is the corresponding locative case form; in 16th- and 17th-century sources an old illative form ā

parole.significato: industrious, hard-working, diligent (who works well, who works a lot)
parole.testo: Derived from an obsolete verb tekt (“to rush, to run, to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- (“to run, to flow”), whence also tecēt (“to flow”); the meaning changed from “moving quickly” to “working hard.” The e → a change parallels tecēt, taka (“path”). parole.significato: liquid (in a state of matter such that it can flow and take the form of its container)
parole.testo: From the same stem as šķīst (“to dissolve, to melt”) (q.v.): Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēi- (“clear, light, shiny”). With an extra suffix -d, it lead to two Proto-Baltic variants, one voiceless (with an extra s-mobile) and one voiced: *skied-, *skaid-, *skid- (whence, with an extra suffix -ru-s, šķidrs

parole.significato: to part, to separate, to divide
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. Cognate with Lithuanian ski̇̀rti.
